meta.claim_boundary: Synthetic persona-conditioned appraisals of simulated experience; not Zurich ED staff preferences or psychological measurements.
meta.quote_selection: One prespecified synthetic interview bundle per scenario-condition-persona cell was independently audited by Codex. Only answers passing grounding and claim-layer checks were eligible; displayed text is a verbatim excerpt.
meta.note: Scores are direct means of verified synthetic appraisal dimensions. Quotes are exact excerpts retained by an independent Codex audit, not human-reviewed material or Zurich ED staff testimony.

personas.name: Team Connector
personas.tagline: Actively maintains shared awareness and treats concise coordination as productive work.

personas.name: Focus Protector
personas.tagline: Protects task continuity and accepts interruptions when their operational value is clear.

personas.name: Patient Advocate
personas.tagline: Prioritizes patient accessibility, explanation, dignity, and continuity across handoffs.

personas.name: Vigilant Monitor
personas.tagline: Scans for weak signals, escalation risk, and gaps in situational awareness.

personas.name: Adaptive Generalist
personas.tagline: Balances competing demands and changes strategy with context rather than following one dominant priority.

quotes: The shift felt defined by a rhythmic oscillation between the nursing work area and the left patient rooms. I wasn't anchored to one spot; instead, I moved back and forth, letting the immediate context dictate whether I needed to coordinate with the team or focus on patient care.
Two moments stood out. First, the missed opportunity with a nurse in the nursing work area when I was transitioning tasks; the lack of proximity meant a potential support link was lost.

Introducing a semi-private coordination nook near the left patient rooms would best support my priorities. It would allow for quick, focused coordination without the need to travel back to the busy nursing work area, reducing travel time and maintaining better task continuity.
The layout felt like a series of distinct zones rather than a unified flow. I spent a lot of time moving between the left patient rooms, the nursing work area, and the shared circulation spaces.

The layout made it hard to protect focus because the circulation areas were also the primary spots for opportunistic contacts. I had to constantly weigh whether a passing colleague was worth engaging with.
I would redesign the NURSTA nurse station to remove the relocated desk obstacle and integrate the standing area more seamlessly with the main flow.

The layout created a tension between coordination and focus. In the nursing work area, I often had to decide whether to engage in optional contacts with doctors or nurses, weighing the timing and relevance.

The limited colleague visibility in the nursing work area was the most difficult feature. Periods of up to 231 seconds with no mutually visible colleagues made it hard to coordinate effectively and increased the strain from interruptions, as I had to actively seek out colleagues.
Improving visibility in the nursing work area would best support my priorities by reducing the need to actively seek colleagues and lowering interruption strain.

The layout feels like a hub-and-spoke system where the COCPIT station is the gravitational center. I spent most of my time shuttling between that central coordination point and the patient rooms or corridor.
The COCPIT coordination station was the most supportive feature. It served as the central hub for bed management and team communication.

Replacing the opaque COCPIT partitions with transparent ones would best support my priorities. This would enhance passive visibility, allowing me to assess colleague availability and context without direct engagement, reducing the need to defer contacts and lowering interruption strain.
The shift felt like a series of deliberate returns to the COCPIT station. I moved between the coordination hub and the patient areas, but the rhythm was defined by coming back to check in.
The layout supported coordination by keeping the COCPIT station as a central, visible hub. However, protecting focus required deliberate choices.

Extending the COCPIT partitions to create more semi-private coordination zones in the circulation areas would best support my priorities. This would allow for better focus protection while still enabling necessary coordination, reducing the need to return to the central station for every interaction.

The shift felt like a rhythmic oscillation between the patient rooms and the coordination hubs. I spent most of my time in the right patient-room area, moving back and forth to the nurse station and the coordination point.
The layout forced a trade-off. When I was in the right patient-room area, I had substantial contact activity but limited colleague visibility, which helped me protect task focus on the patient.

Adding a semi-private huddle space in the corridor or near the patient rooms would support coordination without requiring a trip to the NURSTA. This would reduce the missed opportunities in the circulation area.

I would add transparent partitions or a visual line-of-sight from the patient rooms to the circulation area. This would allow me to maintain focus inside the room while still being visible to colleagues in the corridor, reducing the invisibility problem.
